passages.t: ‘Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy’
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses to speak “to the whole congregation of Israel and tell them: Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy” (verse 2).

“Each of you must respect his mother and father, and you must keep My Sabbaths. I am the LORD your God” (verse 3). “Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods” (verse 4).

A peace offering is to be eaten on the day it is offered or the next. What is left on the third day must be burned (verses 5-8).
passages.hearers:
This chapter is the heart of Leviticus. It is spoken to ‘the whole congregation’. No one is left out: not the priests only, or the men only, or the devout only.

Its first line gives the reason for everything in it. Israel is to be holy because God is holy. Holy means set apart, belonging to God. What the chapter goes on to show is where that holiness is seen. It is seen in how a person treats a parent, a worker, a blind man, a poor neighbor and a foreigner. In this chapter holiness has less to do with being apart from people than with how people are treated.

One short sentence comes back about fifteen times: ‘I am the LORD’, or ‘I am the LORD your God’. It works like a signature. Each command is signed with God's name.

Jewish readers have long noticed that the chapter echoes most of the Ten Commandments. These opening verses name three: parents, the Sabbath and idols. Here the mother is named before the father.

And the chapter mixes what modern readers keep apart. A rule about eating a sacrifice on time stands beside rules about honest wages. Leviticus does not divide worship from the rest of life.
passages.later:
The Ten Commandments begin in the same way: “Honor your father and mother”, and “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:12, 8).

Peter quotes verse 2 to Christians scattered across the Roman world: “But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy’” (1 Peter 1:15-16).
passages.asks: The call to be holy was given to everyone, and it began at home, with a mother and a father. Ask where you have thought of holiness as something for special people or special places. And ask what it would look like in the first relationships of your life.

passages.t: The harvest, the worker, the neighbor
passages.happening:
“When you reap the harvest of your land, you are not to reap to the very edges of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest”. The same goes for the vineyard. “Leave them for the poor and the foreigner” (verses 9-10).

“You must not steal. You must not lie or deceive one another” (verse 11). “You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand” (verse 13). “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God” (verse 14).

In court: “you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly” (verse 15). No slander, and no putting a neighbor's life in danger (verse 16).

“You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor” (verse 17). “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Here holiness goes out into the field, the workplace and the court. Most of these commands protect people with little power.

The farmer is to leave the edges of his field uncut and the dropped grain where it falls. The poor and the foreigner may come and gather it. This is not charity handed down. It is a right built into owning land. The poor work for what they take, and keep their dignity.

A day laborer lived from hand to mouth. He needed tonight what he earned today. So his wage is due before the next morning.

A deaf person cannot hear a curse. A blind person cannot see what is put in his path. They are easy to wrong without being caught. The law answers, ‘you shall fear your God’. God hears and sees what they cannot.

A judge must not lean toward the rich out of fear or toward the poor out of pity. Justice that takes sides is no longer justice.

Then the passage turns inward. Verse 17 forbids hatred ‘in your heart’, where no court can reach. It gives the honest alternative: speak to your neighbor plainly about the wrong. Verse 18 forbids revenge and the grudge, the slow form of revenge.

And then comes the sentence that sums up the rest: ‘love your neighbor as yourself’. In the Old Testament love is more than a feeling. It is loyal, practical commitment. The verses around it show what it looks like: grain left for the poor, wages paid, truth told, justice done, hatred given up. Love here is something a person does.

Jewish teachers held this command at the center. A generation before Jesus, Hillel summed up the law by saying that one should not do to a neighbor what one hates. In the early second century Rabbi Akiva called this verse a great principle of the Torah.
passages.later:
The book of Ruth shows the harvest law at work. Ruth, a poor widow and a foreigner from Moab, says, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain” (Ruth 2:2).

James writes to rich landowners in the words of verse 13: “Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you” (James 5:4).

Asked which commandment is the greatest, Jesus named the love of God, and then this verse: “The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these” (Mark 12:31).

Paul writes, “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (Galatians 5:14). James calls it ‘the royal law’ (James 2:8).
passages.hard:
Who is the neighbor in verse 18? Only a fellow Israelite?

In its first setting, yes. The verse speaks of ‘your people’, and the Hebrew word for neighbor means a fellow member of the community. That has led some to think the command is narrow: love your own.

The chapter itself will not let it stay narrow. Sixteen verses later it takes the same words and gives them to the outsider: “You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself” (verse 34). The two verses are a pair. Whoever heard the first was meant to hear the second.

A teacher of the law once put the question to Jesus: “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10:29). Jesus answered with the story of a man beaten and left on the road. Two religious men passed by. A Samaritan, a member of a people his hearers despised, stopped and cared for him. Jesus then turned the question round. He did not say who counts as a neighbor. He asked which of the three had been one, and said, “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:37). In the Sermon on the Mount he went further: “love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

So the question of who must be loved has an answer that keeps widening: the fellow Israelite, the foreigner next door, the stranger on the road, the enemy.
passages.asks: Love of neighbor in this chapter means leaving something in the field, paying on time, telling the truth and giving up a grudge. Ask which of these is yours to do this week, and for whom. And ask whom you hate ‘in your heart’ while being polite to their face, and what honest word you owe them.

passages.t: Statutes for a people set apart
passages.happening:
“You are to keep My statutes” (verse 19). Israel is not to breed two kinds of animal together, sow a field with two kinds of seed, or wear cloth of two kinds of material.

A case follows about a man who lies with a slave girl promised to another man (verses 20-22). The fruit of a newly planted tree is left for three years, given to God in the fourth, and eaten in the fifth (verses 23-25).

Then a run of short commands. No eating meat with the blood in it; no divination or sorcery (verse 26). No cutting the body for the dead, and no tattoo marks (verse 28). “You must not defile your daughter by making her a prostitute” (verse 29). “You must not turn to mediums or spiritists” (verse 31). “You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
This part of the chapter is the one modern readers find strangest, and some of it is strange because its meaning has been lost.

The ban on mixing seems to mirror Genesis 1, where God makes each thing ‘according to their kinds’, and the line God drew between Israel and the nations. Israel wore its calling in its clothes and sowed it in its fields.

The law of the young tree is a lesson in waiting. The first years of fruit are not taken. The fourth year's fruit goes to God. Only then does the owner eat. A person does not seize everything at once, and the first of what comes belongs to God.

Several commands shut out the religion of Israel's neighbors. Cutting the body in grief was known among them. Mediums claimed to speak with the dead. Israel is to seek God, and no other power.

Verse 29 protects a daughter from her own father, and says that such a wrong corrupts the whole land.

Verse 32 commands honor for the old: stand up when they come in.

The case of the slave girl in verses 20 to 22 belongs to the world of ancient slavery, and it should be read honestly. She is a slave, and she has been promised to one man and used by another. The law does not treat it as adultery, which carried death, ‘because she had not been freed’. The man must bring a guilt offering. The woman is not punished. But she is also not asked what she wanted, and the law does not free her. This is a law for a hard world. It limits a wrong and does not end it.
passages.later:
King Saul broke verse 31 on the night before he died: “Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go and consult her” (1 Samuel 28:7). Isaiah asks the question that lies behind the law: “shouldn’t a people consult their God instead? Why consult the dead on behalf of the living?” (Isaiah 8:19).

Deuteronomy gives the cloth rule in particular: “Do not wear clothes of wool and linen woven together” (Deuteronomy 22:11). Observant Jews keep it today.

Paul keeps the spirit of verse 32: “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father” (1 Timothy 5:1).
passages.hard:
Why is a rule about mixed cloth set beside ‘love your neighbor’? And how do Christians decide which of these laws still apply?

The question is fair, and the chapter itself will not separate the two kinds of law. Christians have answered in more than one way. A long tradition, found in Thomas Aquinas and John Calvin and in many Protestant confessions, divides the law into moral, civil and ceremonial parts. The moral law, such as the love of neighbor, honesty and justice, still binds. Ceremonial laws like the rules about mixing pointed to Israel's being set apart, and were fulfilled in Christ. Civil laws governed Israel as a nation. Others hold that the law of Moses as a whole was a covenant with Israel that has been fulfilled in Christ, and that Christians are bound by its commands as the New Testament takes them up. The love of neighbor is taken up there. The rule about cloth is not. Jewish tradition treats all these commands as binding on Jews.

These notes take no side among these accounts. All of them agree that the rule about mixing meant something for Israel, most likely a daily, visible reminder of order and of being set apart.

A word on verse 28. It stands among laws that shut out the mourning rites and the religion of Israel's neighbors. It is not a statement about the worth of anyone who has a tattoo, and no one should be shamed over one.
passages.asks: Israel let the fruit hang for three years and gave the fourth to God. Ask what you are grasping at too soon. And look at the last command: ask how the old are treated where you live and worship, and who among them you could honor this week by simply giving them your time.

passages.happening:
“When a foreigner resides with you in your land, you must not oppress him. You must treat the foreigner living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God” (verses 33-34).

“You must not use dishonest measures of length, weight, or volume. You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (verses 35-36).

“You must keep all My statutes and all My ordinances and follow them. I am the LORD” (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
The chapter saves one of its greatest commands for the end.

The Hebrew word is ger. It means a person living in Israel who was not born there: someone without land of his own, without a family to stand up for him, and without the standing in law that a native had. Such a person was easy to cheat and easy to push aside.

The law gives him three things. He is not to be oppressed. He is to be treated ‘as native-born’, with the same standing as anyone else. And he is to be loved: ‘love him as yourself’. These are the very words of verse 18. What Israel owed to its own, it owed to the outsider among them.

The reason is memory. ‘For you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.’ Israel knew from the inside what it was to be the outsider: to be feared, used and unprotected. God does not let them forget it. Their own suffering is to make them kind. It is never to become a reason to treat others as they were treated.

The command is given more than once in the law of Moses (Exodus 22:21; Deuteronomy 10:19). It is given here as a command to Israel about how its people were to treat those who lived among them. These notes draw no rule from it for any government or party today. They do say what it asks of every reader: the person near you who does not belong is to be loved as you love yourself.

Then honest scales. In a world with no standard measures, a merchant could keep two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling. The poor and the foreigner, who could least afford it, were the easiest to cheat. So the chapter ends in the marketplace. A holy people gives full measure.

Both commands rest on the same ground: ‘who brought you out of the land of Egypt’. A people rescued from those who wronged them must not wrong others.
passages.later:
Moses says where this love comes from. God “loves the foreigner, giving him food and clothing. So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:18-19).

Exodus had already said it: “You must not exploit or oppress a foreign resident, for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:21).

Proverbs speaks of the scales: “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight” (Proverbs 11:1). The word is the one this book uses for its gravest wrongs.

Jesus counts the welcome given to a stranger as given to himself: “I was a stranger and you took Me in” (Matthew 25:35).
passages.hard:
How far does ‘love him as yourself’ go?

As far as verse 18 goes. The command does not ask only that the foreigner be left alone, or treated correctly. It asks for love, and it measures that love by the care a person takes of himself.

The ger was a resident, a person who had come to live among Israel. Within that setting the command asked a great deal: that the person with no land, no family and no standing be given the same justice and the same love as a brother.

Jesus pressed the command outward, to the stranger on the road and even to the enemy (Luke 10:29-37; Matthew 5:44). And the New Testament turns the memory round for Christians. They are themselves called ‘foreigners’ in the world (1 Peter 1:17). People who know they are guests have reason to be kind to guests.
passages.asks: God told Israel to let the memory of its own hard years make it kind. Ask what you have suffered that could make you gentle toward someone in the same place now. And ask who near you is the outsider, at work, in your street, in your church, and what it would mean this week to treat that person as native-born, and to love them as yourself.
